In the [May 13 episode](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g) of Madrona's *Founded & Funded* podcast, [Matt McIlwain](https://www.madrona.com/team/matt-mcilwain/) interviews [Carina Hong](https://www.linkedin.com/in/carinayunhong/), founder of [Axiom](https://www.axiommath.ai/), about her thesis that formal mathematics is the missing deterministic pillar in a GenAI stack built on probabilistic LLMs and predictive analytics. The 41-minute conversation spans her timeline of verified-AI efforts at Google, DeepMind, OpenAI, and Meta (each one researcher-initiated, each one wound down under commercial pressure), the result Axiom posted on the December 2025 [William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lowell_Putnam_Mathematical_Competition) — the US undergraduate-math contest where median scores are typically 0 or 1 out of 120 — on which Axiom scored a perfect 120/120, the first AI to do so, and what Axiom has been finding as it points Axiom Prover, its [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/)-based prover [[1]](#ref-1), at real hardware circuits that industry-standard formal checkers can't handle.

With help of AI, I've built an **[enriched transcript](#transcript) at the bottom of this post** — Madrona's published transcript, sliced into chapter and topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor's-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.

## My Notes

I love this interview. Carina's central claim that today's GenAI rests on two pillars -- *probabilistic LLMs* and *predictive analytics* -- and needs a third *deterministic pillar* is one of the clearest articulations I've seen of a position I've held for a while: probabilistic AI has to be married to a deterministic verifier before it scales into anything safety-critical. I call it "*give a backbone to LLMs*." [Neurosymbolic AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuro-symbolic_AI) is one academic framing of this idea, a research thread running since the 1980s that the LLM era has revived.

The hardware-verification discussion is particularly close to my heart: two of my early papers were on model-based diagnosis from first principles and on combining heuristic search with a formal system to address the problem [[2]](#ref-2)[[3]](#ref-3). The lesson then was that first principles are required to solve the diagnosis problem precisely, but heuristics (in this case genetic algorithms) are needed to tackle the immense search space that opens up. Today, Lean-style infrastructure can encode the problem formally, and GenAI can handle the search on top. It is exciting to see where this powerful combo will lead us to.

### [0:00:00 — Introduction: the AGI / ASI framing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g&t=0s) {#ch-intro}

#### Matt's opening question: AGI, ASI, or something else?

**Matt McIlwain:** It’s great to be with you, Carina. To me, what’s interesting, having been an investor from day one in [Axiom](https://www.axiommath.ai/), is there are these debates about what is artificial general intelligence (AGI) and what is [artificial super intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence) (ASI). Curious how you define, and whether you choose to define it as AGI or ASI, how you define that, and then we’ll go from there.


### [0:02:01 — Defining AGI: two competing definitions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g&t=121s) {#ch-define-agi}

#### The emotional definition vs. the practical definition

**Carina Hong:** Thanks, Matt. It’s always great to chat with you. I feel like the word AGI actually currently, it has this emotion element in it. It’s the belief that reasoning capability can be so abundant, and that you can have copies of any genius you pick in the world. And it compounds from there. You can have these geniuses work with each other, collaborate, and then ideas fuse between different scientific fields.

And then that capability then trickles down to the day-to-day life, for ordinary Joe to enjoy the same amount of capability and speed of knowledge, discovery, generation, and also applications. So that’s why I think a lot of people when they say, “We are AGI-pilled,” that’s what they mean. They believe that future is going to come.

Then there are also other people who define AGI as more practically. When that capability really flows through everyone’s consumer’s day-to-day life and enterprise workflow, because I think we’re quite ahead in the capability, and there are so many people building applications, which is great, but it’s not like a time that someone, say, in Alabama, would use whatever that is the most state-of-the-art coding model, and say UN code verification tool to build a project that is in their passion. And we’re not there yet.


### [0:04:17 — Math Is AGI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g&t=257s) {#ch-math-is-agi}

#### Matt's provocation and Carina's Curry–Howard answer

**Matt McIlwain:** Yeah. I was just in Georgia, and I think people are using the state-of-the-art of AI without realizing they’re using the state-of-the-art of AI. And of course, as you know, and we’ll talk about, the state-of-the-art is moving rapidly.

**Carina Hong:** That’s right.

**Matt McIlwain:** So you’ve made this provocative statement that math is AGI. What does that mean? And what should we take about the statement?

**Carina Hong:** Yeah, I think that is the DNA of Axiom. We’re very clear that, in the future, we’re going to see so many promising markets. The first one is best versus verification. In the future, we’re going to see more markets, but the DNA of the company remains math. And in our view, we think that from math and code, which, if you understand it in a sort of [Curry-Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence) way, are actually twins. You can then do a lot of things in the kind of use software and generation verification to control things that are in the real world, like physical engineering stuff. And then you can go to everything else. So from our worldview, math is AGI because that is the starting point of reasoning.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The [Curry–Howard correspondence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curry%E2%80%93Howard_correspondence) is the observation that proofs and programs are the same object seen from two sides: a proof of a theorem *is* a program, and the theorem *is* that program's type. Lean (and other dependently-typed provers) make this literal — proofs are written as programs and checked by the type-checker. That's why Carina calls math and code "twins": in a Curry–Howard setting, verifying a program is identical to proving a theorem about it.
:::

A lot of other people have different definitions of AGI. I would say that if you take the view that math is AGI, you have your action plan, you execute that a lot faster, because math is a lot cleaner. So, I was on this AI for science conference in San Francisco. It’s a really great panel, and everyone is doing experiments with the physical world. And obviously, the latency of iteration is quite long. In math, just like in coding, the digital world, your iteration time is a lot shorter.

And the other thing that’s really interesting is that because math is data-scarce compared to the other domains. So you hit some of the roadblocks a lot faster, which allows you to debug those roadblocks. So that’s, I think, one interesting difference between math and coding. With coding, we were able to make a lot of progress at the start locally, just because there’s a lot of coding data.

**Matt McIlwain:** There’s a ton of data, yeah.

**Carina Hong:** That’s right.

**Matt McIlwain:** Repositories everywhere.

**Carina Hong:** And that’s just massive amounts of data compared to, say, informal math data, or formal math data, which is even smaller.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The "formal vs. informal math" split is central to this interview, so it's worth spelling out what each side means in context.

*Informal math* is math written in natural language: textbook proofs, research papers, chain-of-thought reasoning [[4]](#ref-4) labeled by graders, and step-by-step solutions scraped from the web. The corpus is huge and growing. It's what general-purpose LLMs (GPT-4, o1, DeepSeek, Gemini) learn their math ability from. Correctness is judged by humans or by other LLMs — there's no machine check that a given proof step follows from the previous one.

*Formal math* is math written in a machine-checkable proof language — [Lean 4](https://lean-lang.org/) [[1]](#ref-1) in Axiom's case, but also Coq, Isabelle, and HOL. Every proof step type-checks against the underlying logic, so there's zero ambiguity about whether a proof is correct. The tradeoff is that the corpus is tiny — [mathlib](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/) (Lean's canonical math library) has to be hand-written, and most undergraduate mathematics isn't formalized yet. Axiom Prover, AlphaProof, and the earlier HOList [[5]](#ref-5) / GPT-f [[6]](#ref-6) lines all operate in this mode.

The "religious" divide Carina describes: formal-camp researchers think informal-math LLMs can't scale without verification because hallucinated proofs look fluent; informal-camp researchers think formal is a niche dead-end because the corpus is too small to train anything capable. Her reconciliation — "iron sharpens iron" via Draft, Sketch, and Prove [[7]](#ref-7) — is that informal LLMs draft candidate proofs, and a formal prover fills in and verifies the steps, so better informal reasoners directly help formal ones.
:::


### [0:06:12 — Math data scarcity as a feature, not a bug](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g&t=372s) {#ch-math-data-scarcity}

**Matt McIlwain:** Yeah, say more about this math scarcity, data scarcity issue, because I think that that’s one of the areas that you all are creatively trying to address.

#### Informal math stalls above high school; Axiom's bet on invented structured data

**Carina Hong:** That’s right. So, math is such a data-scarce domain. I think a lot of researchers at the beginning were kind of blindsided by the idea that, well, we just take whatever has more data in math, and take that research path, which is informal math. So what they do is they start scraping textbooks, and papers, and chain of thought reasoning data [[4]](#ref-4) through expert data labeling companies. And they try to basically build a math model that way.

It worked for a bit. So, it worked for, say, high school level, where you really just have a lot of data. And it’s a lot easier to say find human experts around the world at the high school, international math Olympia level, than say at the postdoc, or junior researcher, algebraic geometry level.

We thought a bit more first principally. We were like, “Well, we think we need structured data.” And even if that means there isn’t a lot of structured data right now, how do we invent to create structured data?

Instead of going to the unstructured route, because today we have a lot more unstructured than structured. And the structured data looks a lot like code.

I mean, it’s mostly written in the theorem-proving language called [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/), which has its own history, that’s separate from the deep learning development timeline.

And just wasn’t any Lean data. And people had to hand-code the undergraduate textbooks. They start with algebra, and then they did analysis. I remember this was 2020. I was at MIT. Fast-forward to, I think we started July last year. And we started under the belief that we can try to make progress on formal proving pretty fast. We were unclear what was the moment that formal math can catch up to informal math.


### [0:08:13 — Formal vs. informal math — "it's almost like a religion"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g&t=493s) {#ch-formal-vs-informal}

**Matt McIlwain:** So take us a little bit, because there’s, I think, two interesting things here. One is this idea of formal and informal AI. Let’s unpack that.

#### "It's almost like a religion": why RL-for-coding researchers join the formal camp

**Carina Hong:** People just debate about it. And I cannot convince someone who does informal math to look at the formal math. I’m like, “You’re missing out.” Really are. And it’s usually the people who are working on [reinforcement learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning) for other domains, like coding. They know that if you do RLVR [reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards] [[8]](#ref-8), it’s incredible, they know that math is most interesting when it’s proofs, and it’s most interesting if you assign reward for the proof instead of just a numerical answer. So, they tend to join this movement.

**Matt McIlwain:** Some people ask the question, “Why now? Why is this all important today?” And I usually start with, well, in a world where we’re building these LLMs [large language models], which by definition are non-deterministic, they’re predictive systems, you need some kind of system that’s a prover, that’s a verifier. How do you think about that on the why now question?

#### Why now: AlphaProof's MCTS, Draft-Sketch-Prove, and iron-sharpens-iron

**Carina Hong:** So, first of all, we could not have been early. I think that’s right. Because we’re seeing the… I mean, informal is doing pretty well. It’s at a time when we needed to get started to play catch-up in the data-scarce domain.

I think around the time of 2024, there’s this amazing achievement of [AlphaProof](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/ai-solves-imo-problems-at-silver-medal-level/). And they use something called [Monte Carlo Tree Search](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_tree_search). That is quite an expensive system for a startup, expensive method for a startup to do.

It was not clear to me that was the only way. Now, in terms of why the urge to make it happen, both from my perspective and a lot of others who join us, I think it was at a time when people had more faith in structured data.

So, I think if we talk about the latter half of 2024, people thought about coding as just another enterprise application. Coding is no different from developing an AI financial analyst. It’s no different from developing an AI McKinsey consultant.

Now, obviously, we know now coding’s a lot different than that. I don’t want to talk about [recursive self-improvement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recursive_self-improvement), but perhaps if you can agree on, at least, that is like autocatalytic. So, coding does have that advantage.

We’re not far, I think, from [building an AI that can do AI research](/posts/20260508-import-ai-455-automating-ai-research/). Now, the definition of that is very loose.

You can define that as getting publications, or even spotlight papers, and [ICLR](https://iclr.cc/), [ICML](https://icml.cc/), [NeurIPS](https://neurips.cc/). You can also define that as being as good as one of those researchers out there at frontier labs.

**Matt McIlwain:** Yes. And some of the great researchers in academia, I was talking with our mutual friend, [Carlos Guestrin](https://guestrin.su.domains/), and he and some of his teams have been working on some of this area of continuous learning with reinforcement learning.

**Carina Hong:** Yeah. But I’m sort of fortunate and grateful that the RL coding community, they do strengthen humanity space in this other religion. And I think that’s one reason. So the code gen development. The other is the informal reasoner getting stronger, which actually also helps us. In the AI for math community, there’s this paper called "Draft, Sketch, and Prove." [[7]](#ref-7) The idea is after you produce an informal proof, and you try to produce a Lean sketch, and you try to fill in the stories that are the voids of the Lean sketch, it works better. Now, the first part is obviously beneficial if the informal models are doing better. So, September 2024 was [o1](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/).

**Matt McIlwain:** And so in a sense, it’s iron sharpens iron. They’re making each other better.

#### Lean 4 workability and AXLE, the Axiom Lean Engine

**Carina Hong:** That is correct. And I think that is something that Axiom can talk about a lot and a lot, right? And we’re not talking about the only formal Monte Carlo Tree Search rigid stiff approach. I do think that we are able to get the benefits of both systems. And I think the third thing is just like after September 2023, [Lean 4](https://lean-lang.org/lean4/doc/whatIsLean.html) becomes a lot more workable from an engineering perspective. It is still surprisingly not workable. That’s why we built [AXLE, Axiom Lean Engine](https://www.axiommath.ai/axle), which is this sort of infrastructure. There are a dozen tools, and we’re adding tools to it on a weekly basis. I believe there are people around the world, literally all across the world, using it. And people are using it interestingly with their favorite model. We see the choice of literally any model. It can be a large language model that’s off the shelf, it can be the specialized model. Even some of our competitors’ models.

**Matt McIlwain:** I love this.

**Carina Hong:** But they use all these models with the infrastructure of AXLE because it does solve a pain point that Lean is slow.

**Matt McIlwain:** We were together the week you launched AXLE. And it’s incredible to see the progress.

**Carina Hong:** Yeah. The growth curve of the user metric is quite high.

**Matt McIlwain:** And I think it’s at building that ecosystem out where the iron is sharpening iron that is, I think, going to help the whole community benefit. I love that framing. And I think for some of the folks in the audience that are saying, okay, how much is this getting applied, or beginning to be applied? This tension as it were between math proofs and coding. There are companies, big companies in some cases like the Amazons and Googles that are already working on this area. You’re a little bit familiar with that. ### [0:13:44 — Google, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta all abandoned formal math](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g&t=824s) {#ch-abandoned-formal}

#### Carina's timeline: Google 2016 (HOL-Light), DeepMind 2021 (AlphaGeometry intern)

**Carina Hong:** So, I think, I certainly draw a timeline of verified AI. So 2016, Google made a pretty important bottoms-up strategic investment. There are good papers coming out of it. Playing with a language, they’re improving language called [HOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOL_(proof_assistant)) [higher-order logic]. HOL List [[5]](#ref-5) is one of the papers. And then there are white papers [[5]](#ref-5)[[9]](#ref-9), I think in 2019 by [Christian Szegedy](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3QeF7mAAAAAJ), a friend of mine, when he and Tony Wu, who later became [xAI](https://x.ai/)’s co-founder, that was like 2016, 2019. And then that’s Google, right? Mothership.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor’s note.** "HOL List" is likely a reference to HOList [[5]](#ref-5), the Google-led 2019 paper that set up an automated-theorem-proving environment over the HOL Light library, with Christian Szegedy as a co-author. "Tony Wu, who later became xAI’s co-founder" refers to [Yuhuai "Tony" Wu](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~ywu/), who joined xAI as a founding member — xAI’s [public founding team](https://x.ai/about) lists him among the initial researchers rather than as a corporate co-founder in the CEO-equivalent sense. The Szegedy / Wu collaboration on HOList and the 2020 "Mathematical Reasoning via Self-supervised Skip-tree Training" [[9]](#ref-9) paper is what Carina’s timeline points to.
:::

And then 2021 was [DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/). Also bottoms up effort. One intern decides to apply this geometry. It’s just personal hobby. So, when this person was a high schooler, he has no interest in the other Math Olympiad problems compared to his interest for geometry. So he just said, “I just want to do geometry.” And that’s such a smart idea.

I sometimes think of it, because when I was a kid, I could never solve the geometry problem on the Math Olympiad in the geometric way. There’s something about my brain, and I think it’s still like now, I don’t have any sense of direction, I can’t envision spatial objects. I can’t do topology in the visual way. When I was studying geometry, I couldn’t picture those curves and surfaces. It’s almost like my brain is inhibited in that way.

On the other hand, I overcompensate by being the strongest algebraic brute force person you can find. I mean, when I was a kid, I would eat all the inequality problems.

So, from a strategic point of view, I just figured out that I can express all these lines, points, intersection points, circles, triangles, in complex coordinates, and this is a brute force method. So then I just throw away that picture. I just look at work with this complex coordinates, and I do it the algebraic way. And it would took me three times the time.

But it tells you something philosophical. That’s not quite exactly the AI corresponding thing, but it’s like, if you have a geometric figure, you can try to express it in a symbolic language, for both that human kid, and in this case, this intern of Google DeepMind, who then that was a wildly successful project [[AlphaGeometry](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/alphageometry-an-olympiad-level-ai-system-for-geometry/)].

They expressed the geometry problem in the vector language, not Lean, even more smaller domain specific vector language. So, all these pictures suddenly become computer code.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The intern-driven geometry project is AlphaGeometry, led at DeepMind by Trieu H. Trinh during his internship and eventually published in *Nature* (January 2024) [[10]](#ref-10). Carina says "the vector language, not Lean" — AlphaGeometry 1 used a bespoke geometry-specific domain language, not Lean; its successor AlphaProof, released in July 2024 for IMO 2024, is the one that runs in Lean.
:::

I think they later gave up on it. I don’t really quite know. After Alphaproof, it was such a success. And so somehow the informal math team, Gemini had the mainstream voice and the non-lean approach, which is Gemini post-training, took over, they started develop evolve, that is discovery, construction not proving. So we didn’t quite hear much from them.

**Matt McIlwain:** Well, I think they got pulled a little bit given some of the new model companies that were making such good progress, and they had to focus for a season on the here and now, which of course creates the opportunity for Axiom Math. So, where do we go from here? Where does the field go, and then where does Axiom Math go?

**Carina Hong:** I still think sometimes it’s just so interesting to think about why things stopped at each of these players.

**Matt McIlwain:** Yeah, that’s an interesting question.

#### OpenAI (GPT-f, Stan Polu, Elon-left) and Meta (Llama → Mistral)

**Carina Hong:** And we just covered the Google story. The [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) story was just like, when Elon was there, with [Stan Polu](https://polu.st/) and other folks, they had so many papers. That was frequent within a couple months. Meaning [miniF2F](https://github.com/openai/miniF2F) was the high school benchmark they established. That was later sort of really trained on, contaminated by everyone, but it was one of the initial benchmarks pointing at least a direction to go. I think there was GPT-f [[6]](#ref-6). They tried to have early version GPT to maybe stand for mathematical functions, I think. And then they just didn’t… I mean, Elon left. They just wasn’t supported.

Facebook was doing it. Facebook was doing it. The [Llama](https://www.llama.com/) team, they spun out to be [Mistral](https://mistral.ai/), and that was the end of story. I mean, there was [Guillaume Lample](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ptx1FUUAAAAJ), there was [Fabian](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XvB37d4AAAAJ). You still see some of the bottoms up Meta researchers, but not really feeling like AI from X was supported. So they came to Axiom. Yeah, great opportunity.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The framing collapses two distinct teams. The Llama project at Meta / FAIR spun out some people, but Mistral was co-founded by Arthur Mensch (ex-DeepMind, not a Llama lead), Guillaume Lample (ex-FAIR, worked on LLaMA and earlier on formal math with Fabian Gloeckle), and Timothée Lacroix (ex-FAIR) — not the Llama team en bloc. "Fabian" is likely [Fabian Gloeckle](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XvB37d4AAAAJ), who co-authored the formal-math work at FAIR (HyperTree Proof Search and related) with Lample; Gloeckle remained at Meta after Lample left.
:::

But you just see kind of how short-lived each of these excellent projects are in the big places.

**Matt McIlwain:** I think that probably in some of these places the research had to be in service of what ultimately became the commercial pressures. And that perhaps, a few years back, the commercial opportunity to have provers that are the complementary tension to systems that are predictors, was not quite ready for prime time. But now it is.

**Carina Hong:** But why did they start it? So that’s kind of my…

**Matt McIlwain:** Well, I think they knew that it would come.

**Carina Hong:** I see.

**Matt McIlwain:** And it was maybe a timing question.

**Carina Hong:** Oh, they did it too early?

The Dwarkesh appearance built on the call Sutskever first made publicly at his [NeurIPS 2024 Test of Time talk](/posts/20241213-sutskever-pretraining-over/) — "pre-training as we know it will end." *Continual learning* is the ability for a model to keep absorbing new information after pretraining without forgetting what it already knew (the classic failure mode is "catastrophic forgetting"). Today's frontier LLMs are frozen after training: post-training fine-tunes them but doesn't let them learn from interactions in deployment. The "Ilya surge" Carina names is the wave of seed-stage startup pitches that picked up that framing in the months following the podcast.

### [0:38:03 — What autonomous proof generation looks like: the Ramanujan tau result](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wcgQr7qQd9g&t=2283s) {#ch-autonomous-proof}

#### Ramanujan tau function misses 100% of the primes — autonomously proved by Axiom Prover

**Carina Hong:** I don’t know if the last time I saw you, I told you this news, but just their mathematical results, that after I tell people, they’re like, “I don’t really know how to technically prove it, but it sounds beautiful.” And here’s one. It’s something recently autonomously proved by Axiom Prover. So, the [Ramanujan tau function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan_tau_function) is tau, and it is a function that appears frequently in [Ramanujan's lost notebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%27s_lost_notebook). It’s one of the fundamental functions in number theory. Axiom Prover, the AI, autonomously proved that the Ramanujan tau function misses 100% of the primes.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** "Misses 100% of the primes" is a *density* statement, not a pointwise one. The open problem Carina is gesturing at is [Lehmer's 1947 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan_tau_function) that $\tau(n) \neq 0$ for every positive integer $n$ — verified by computation up to $n \approx 8.16 \times 10^{23}$ (Derickx) but still unproved in general. The density version, "the set of primes $p$ at which $\tau(p) = 0$ has natural density zero," is meaningful progress toward Lehmer rather than Lehmer itself, and Carina's conditioning on the [ABC conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture) in the next turn is essential, not decorative.
:::

**Matt McIlwain:** Wow.

#### ABC conjecture caveat; Mirzakhani, Alex Wright, and seven arXiv papers

**Carina Hong:** And this is assuming the [ABC conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture), of course, which is something like the [Ramanujan hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramanujan%E2%80%93Petersson_conjecture); a lot of people, or generalized people, just agree or assume all, but this is something that we don’t know. And so that is a beautiful result. I mean, just when we shared it, people felt like that is… I like to be this math evangelist, because I just like talking about it. Relatedly, there are mathematicians like Ramanujan in this case and [Maryam Mirzakhani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryam_Mirzakhani). They left behind bodies of work in terms of Mirzakhani, there is the dynamical systems. And recently, there is a paper that we published, in which Michigan Professor [Alex Wright](https://public.websites.umich.edu/~alexmw/) posed the problem. And in that case, we were able to also formalize the solution. So, verify it is correct, and actually optimize the proof and correct the proof mistakes. So, comes in different forms, some autonomous proving, some auto formalization, but we are at a point where we have, I think, seven papers on archived [arXiv] now, where the main engine is done by Axiom Prover. I think five for proving, and two for other formalizations.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The analogy between the ABC conjecture and the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture ("Ramanujan hypothesis") is loose. Both are deep open problems that much of modern number theory assumes, but they are about different objects. ABC is a statement about additive relations among the prime factors of integers satisfying $a + b = c$, while Ramanujan–Petersson bounds the size of the Fourier coefficients of modular forms. Carina's "assumed by many, still unproved" framing is fair, but the equivalence between the two is not.
:::

**Matt McIlwain:** Well, I’m excited about this idea of the beauty of math, and the applied beauty of math that Axiom, you, Carina, and your team are going to help us discover in the years ahead.

**Carina Hong:** Thanks, Matt.

**Matt McIlwain:** So thanks so much for being here with me today.

**Carina Hong:** It’s really great.

**Matt McIlwain:** I really enjoyed the conversation.

**Carina Hong:** Thank you.

## Related Posts

- [Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search](/posts/20260606-ai-formal-proof-search/): a large-scale test of the same AlphaProof-in-Lean approach Axiom builds on, closing open Erdős and OEIS problems.
- [When Computers Write Proofs, What's the Point of Mathematicians?](/posts/20230902-computers-write-proofs/): the earlier framing of the formal-proving question Carina's "math is AGI" thesis answers from a startup's vantage.
- [The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics](/posts/20260602-leiden-declaration-ai-mathematics/): the mathematics community asking for guardrails around exactly the AI-proving capability Axiom is racing to commercialize.
- [Even Experts Are Surprised by AI's Latest 'Vibe-Mathing' Advance](/posts/20260427-chatgpt-vibe-math-proof/): the informal-math counterweight to Axiom's formal-verification bet, where an LLM advances math without a machine-checked proof.
- [Sutskever at NeurIPS 2024: Pre-Training Era Is Over](/posts/20241213-sutskever-pretraining-over/): the source of the "scaling is dead, long live scaling" framing Carina invokes for her structured-data pitch.
